records.derivation: Use coordinates [0,8]^2 and coin radius r=1/2. Complete containment makes its center range over [1/2,15/2]^2, of area 49. The central black diamond has vertices (4,2),(6,4),(4,6),(2,4), area 8, and perimeter 8*sqrt(2). Centers within distance r of it consist of the diamond, four outward strips of total area perimeter*r=4*sqrt(2), and four quarter-disks of total area pi/4. Their area is 8+4*sqrt(2)+pi/4; all of this set stays inside the feasible-center square. For the lower-left black triangle, a feasible center hits it exactly when x+y<=2+sqrt(2)/2. Indeed the perpendicular foot on its hypotenuse belongs to that segment: x,y>=1/2 and this bound imply |x-y|<2. Put u=x-1/2,v=y-1/2. The center-hit region is a right triangle u,v>=0, u+v<=1+sqrt(2)/2. All four corner regions therefore have area 4*(1/2)*(1+sqrt(2)/2)^2=3+2*sqrt(2). They are mutually disjoint. They also do not meet the central expanded region: the corresponding closest parallel black edges have distance 2*sqrt(2), exceeding twice r=1. Thus the favorable center area is 11+6*sqrt(2)+pi/4, and its probability under the ordinary uniform-center model is (44+24*sqrt(2)+pi)/196. Hence a+b=68, C. Boundaries have area zero.
records.scopeExplanation: Geometric probability supplies the model. The finite-radius placement region is explicitly derived by perpendicular distances, triangles, rectangular strips and sectors; no general offset-body formula or new placement theorem is assumed.
records.routeAssumptions: Use the exact stated geometry, legal moves, domain or random model as explained in the complete derivation; no optional advanced theorem is universalized.
answerAssumptions: The probability uses the ordinary uniform-area distribution of the feasible coin center; the displayed random-location wording does not explicitly specify its density.

records.derivation: Represent a position by the sorted tuple of its nonempty wall lengths, together with the player to move. A legal move chooses a wall of length n, removes k=1 or 2 consecutive bricks, and leaves wall lengths l and n-k-l, for every integer 0<=l<=n-k; zero lengths are dropped. Existing other walls are unchanged. Sorting loses no legal information because wall locations and orientations do not affect later choices. Every move strictly decreases the total number of bricks. The empty position is losing for the player to move because the preceding player has removed the last brick. For each increasing brick total, declare a state winning if it has a legal successor already proved losing, and losing if every legal successor is proved winning. Induction on the total proves this rule gives a guaranteed strategy, not a random-play probability. The attached exact certificate includes all 79 states reachable from the five choices, every distinct legal successor, and a move to a losing state for each winning state. It classifies choices A,C,D,E as winning for Arjun and B=(1,2,6) as losing. B has nine distinct legal successors, all winning for Beth to move. Example winning moves from the other choices are A->(1,1,1,4), C->(1,2,2,4), D->(1,1,3,3), and E->(1,2,6). Beth can therefore guarantee a win exactly for B. Both actual images illustrate the same one-wall removal and possible splitting rule. No Sprague-Grundy values, xor-composition theorem or extrapolated periodic pattern is used.
records.scopeExplanation: The existing finite-pile-game definition explicitly requires the actual removal/terminal rules in the state and gives both existential winning moves and universal losing-state conditions. A wall configuration is a finite brick-removal state under those stated rules. The direct full-state certificate applies those exact criteria; it does not widen the count/probability recursion scope or silently insert a disjoint-sum theorem.

records.derivation: Scale AB to1, put A=(0,0), B=(1,0), and take P=(x,y) in the unit square above AB. The perpendicular bisector x=1/2 separates AP<BP on the left from AP>BP on the right. The quarter unit disk D centered at A is AP<AB. Thus AP is the middle side exactly in (D intersect {x>1/2}) union ({x<1/2} outside D), apart from zero-area equalities. Let L be the area of D with x<1/2. The circle meets x=1/2 at (1/2,sqrt(3)/2), by Pythagoras. The region L splits into a 30-degree unit sector of area pi/12 and a right triangle of area sqrt(3)/8, so L=pi/12+sqrt(3)/8. The favorable area is (pi/4-L)+(1/2-L)=(6+pi-3*sqrt(3))/12. The coefficients are a=6,b=1,c=3,d=3,e=12, with gcd(6,1,3,12)=1 and squarefree d=3; their sum is25, A.

records.derivation: The three independent uniform numbers give a uniform point (x,y,z) in the unit cube. For a specified coordinate x to exceed twice both others, the region is 0<x<1, 0<=y<x/2, 0<=z<x/2. It is the pyramid with apex (0,0,0) and square base {x=1,0<=y,z<=1/2}, so its volume is (1/3)*1*(1/4)=1/12. The analogous y-largest and z-largest events are disjoint: two distinct nonnegative coordinates cannot each exceed twice the other. Their union is precisely the requested event. Add the three pyramid volumes to obtain 3/12=1/4, E. All boundaries have zero volume under the explicitly supplied continuous model.

records.derivation: The original denominator excludes all its real roots, even when a numerator factor cancels. In a nonpositive set [a,b] union (c,d), a<b<c<d, the closed endpoints a,b must be numerator zeros not excluded by the denominator, and the open endpoints c,d must be denominator zeros. All four endpoints belong to {1,2,3,4,5}. Monicity and degree3 then leave one extra factor in each polynomial. To preserve the required signs and endpoint types, these factors must be the same (x-t): otherwise one gains an extra sign boundary or isolated zero, or changes a prescribed endpoint type. Write P=(x-a)(x-b)(x-t), Q=(x-c)(x-d)(x-t). The choices t=c and t=d are always valid, and define exactly the same function on exactly the same natural domain R minus {c,d}; they must not be counted twice as functions. A third possibility is the unused fifth integer e, but only if its removable hole lies outside the required nonpositive set. This happens for unused e=1,3,5, and fails for e=2 or4 because that hole would cut one of the required intervals. There are five ordered endpoint quadruples, giving five base functions, plus three distinct additional-domain-hole functions, hence eight distinct natural-domain functions. If removable holes are entirely disregarded in function identity, the count instead becomes five; that convention also gives no listed option. The source13 counts polynomial-pair representations: two for each of the five endpoint quadruples plus the three allowable unused-root representations. For a concrete duplicate, (P,Q)=((x-1)(x-2)(x-3),(x-3)^2(x-4)) and ((x-1)(x-2)(x-4),(x-3)(x-4)^2) both define (x-1)(x-2)/((x-3)(x-4)) on R minus {3,4}, with nonpositive set [1,2] union (3,4). The exact certificate independently enumerates all35*35=1225 monic cubic pairs from root multisets, evaluates every real sign cell and root-domain point using rational arithmetic, and confirms13 eligible pairs,8 natural-domain function classes and5 reduced expressions. None of the listed choices is the function count under either stated convention.
